This is a RFC related to array API.

The central question is: who knows best when to run a computation on the CPU vs on a GPU/accelerated hardware?

So far we've been assuming that the user will know when to move data from one device to the other. As a result we need something like the [`MoveTo` transformer](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33737). There are probably other things that result from this assumption, but I can't think of them right now.

Inspired by using [sentence-transformers](https://sbert.net/) and realising that it automatically uses my GPU when I run the code on a machine with a GPU, the MPS device of my MacBook and otherwise stays on the CPU. This was a cool experience because I didn't have to go and edit my code. The input to sentence-transformers was always a Numpy array but it knew that if there was a CUDA device it made sense to use it. From talking about this with Olivier I learnt that TabICL also does this (the processing starts on the CPU but it then moves to the GPU).

Roughly at the same time I investigated how long it takes to move different amounts of data from CPU memory to GPU memory (and back). Some results and the script used to measure it https://gist.github.com/betatim/f4128b961525eda49df9b76c7c339388 (ignore the "predicted" column, it isn't that useful). The main thing I took away from this is that even fairly large datasets take about half a second. Combined with my assumption that the work that happens in the estimator takes at least a second or two and sometimes much longer it made me think "if this is true then moving data is 'cheap'". I'm not 100% there isn't a mistake or logic error here. Let me know what you think.

The result from that discussion and the transfer time experiment is this RFC.

The proposal is that an estimator is allowed to move from one namespace/device to another if it thinks that it makes sense to do so. So for example you feed a numpy array to `Ridge` which then decides to move to pytorch and the GPU to do the computation. This behaviour would be controlled by a global setting (opt-in at the start). Each estimator probably also needs to have some public API to control its behaviour.

It would remove the need for having a `MoveTo` transformer and free the user from having to think about this/know when best to transition from one namespace/device to another. It would also make it easier to have code for a pipeline that works on a machine with and without a GPU - no need to edit the code.

We already kinda do this for some (parts of some) estimators. Mostly we do it because there is no array API function to do what we want to do, but there is a Numpy one. Internally the estimator moves the data to numpy, performs the computation and then moves the result back (if needed).

We'd have to have some "order of precedence" function that knows how to check if cupy, pytorch, dpnp are installed, if there is an accelerator present that is supported by the installed library and then decided what to do. I think in practice this is not that complicated as most machines will only have one type of accelerator and one of these libraries installed. I think sentence-transformers uses PyTorch and then: CUDA > MPS > CPU ([for example here](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/main/sentence_transformers/util/environment.py#L40) and then used [here](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/main/sentence_transformers/base/model.py#L182))

Overall I think this would be a nice UX for users if it doesn't become "too magical".

What do people think?

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

If passing multi-class data to a classifier where some class has only observations with zero weights, estimators will produce odd solutions which do not really make sense.

For example:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(30, 3))
y = rng.integers(3, size=X.shape[0])
w = rng.standard_gamma(1, size=X.shape[0])
w[y == 1] = 0.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
LogisticRegression().fit(X, y, w).coef_
```
```
array([[-0.01295201,  0.04689646, -0.19975591],
       [ 0.0006037 ,  0.00044906,  0.00039081],
       [ 0.01234832, -0.04734552,  0.19936509]])
```

Mathematically, the correct solution would be something with a minus infinite as intercept and zeros in all coefficients, and the same applies to other classifiers with intercepts (e.g. gradient boosters), but I don't think this would be a desirable solution.

Technically, the sample weights according to the documentation should be interpreted as if each observation would be repeated the amount of times given by the weights, and if we take that as zero, that means leaving them out, in which case the classes with zero weights would be removed during the pre-processing and would not be available under `model.classes_`.

But that sort of behavior would be quite problematic for other libraries that aim at providing scikit-learn-compatible interfaces - for example, it'd contradict the docs that instruct developers to call `np.unique` to get the classes ([link](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimator-types)), and if implemented in such a way that [validate_data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data.html) could return something with different shape than the input, it might require other scikit-learn-compatible libraries to have a hard dependency on scikit-learn, and would likely break many things if the shapes differ.

Thus, I think the most reasonable behavior here would be to error out with an informative message.

For reference, this is what GLMNET would do, and would even have a non-zero threshold for it which is perhaps a more reasonable way of handling it:
```r
library(glmnet)
data("iris")
x <- iris[, -5]
y <- iris$Species
w <- rep(1, length(y))
w[y == "virginica"] <- 0
glmnet(x, y, weights=w, family="multinomial")
```
```
Error: from glmnet C++ code (error code 8003); Null probability for class 3 < 1.0e-5
```

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I want to cluster high-dimensional sparse data to return **sparse centroids**. Typically a TF-IDF transform over a vocab of 10K to 100K.  

Today `MiniBatchKMeans` returns dense centroids with low nnz even when the data is 99% sparse.  


#### Benefits:
1. **Memory.** with `n_clusters=10_000` and `n_features=100_000` that cluster centers array would be 80GB alone which with 90% sparsity would become 8GB. It is what the Sculley paper designed `MiniBatchKMeans` to handle.  
2. **Fit cost.** Projection adds <5% to fit time. 95% sparse centroids means 95% fewer multiply-adds per assignment dot product. Turning that into wall-time requires the assignment loop to skip zero centroid entries (same pattern as `lloyd_iter_chunked_sparse`), which is a follow-on in the PR.

3. **Interpretability.** A sparse centroids with 50 nnz is intuitively easier to understand than one with `10_000`.

```python
mbk = MiniBatchKMeans(l1_radius=1).fit(X_tfidf)
mbk.cluster_centers_ # dense ndarray, but 90% are exactly 0.0

```
`l1_radius` being the radius of L1 ball that after each iteration the centroids gets projected on to.  
The idea is from Sculley 2010, where MiniBatchKMeans itself comes from.  
This would cause the centroids to be sparse which is useful for scaling and a natural fit for already sparse data(e.g. TF-IDF transformed text).  
Besides that it can also act as mild regularization.

Sketch of expected empirical impact (preliminary; concrete benchmark belongs in the PR):     
 - 20 Newsgroups TF-IDF, k=20, p~=24,000: at l1_radius=3.0, centroid sparsity rises from ~0%   
 to ~87% with `adjusted_mutual_info_score` ~1% better than plain MiniBatchKMeans.
 - RCV1 train split, k=4, p~=47,000: centroid sparsity ~96% at l1_radius=3.0, negligible       
 AMI/ARI delta.

### Describe your proposed solution

Add one optional parameter, `l1_radius` `float` or `None`, that defaults to `None` to `MiniBatchKMeans`.  
When `None` the estimator behaves the same way as today.  
When set to `r` every centroid update is followed by a Euclidean projection of each centroid onto L1 ball ${x: norm_1(x) <= r}$.  
This is from Section 5 of Sculley(2010), cited as the basis of `MiniBatchKMeans` itself in sklearn docs.  

#### Where would the change go:
After the EMA update inside `_minibatch_update_dense` / `_minibatch_update_sparse`, apply the projection to each updated row of `centers_new` before  sklearn's convergence diff is computed.                                                      

#### Projection Algorithm:
The exact `O(p log p)` sort-based method of Duchi et al. (ICML 2008, Algorithm 1). A numpy implementation would look like this:
```python
   def project_l1_ball(v, kappa):                                                             
       abs_v = np.abs(v)                                                                      
       if abs_v.sum() <= kappa:                                                               
           return v.copy()                                                                    
       u = np.sort(abs_v)[::-1]                                                               
       cssv = np.cumsum(u) - kappa                                                            
       rho = np.nonzero(u * np.arange(1, v.size + 1) > cssv)[0][-1]                           
       theta = cssv[rho] / (rho + 1)                                                          
       return np.sign(v) * np.maximum(abs_v - theta, 0.0)                                     
```
In my experiments with 20 Newsgroups TF-IDF(`p=24000`, `k=20`) the projection is well below 5% of fit time.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

1. **Posthoc soft thresholding.** Fit plain `MiniBatchKMeans`, then project centroids once at the end. Not equivalent: per iteration keeps centroids sparse *during* training, so assignments see sparse centroids and the storage/fit time benefits kick in immediately. Posthoc only sparsifies at inference. Quality is dataset dependent. On 20 Newsgroups (k=20, r=3.0) per iteration AMI=0.307 vs posthoc 0.306 (baseline 0.303). On RCV1 (k=4) they are within noise. Per iteration is the algorithm as Sculley section 5 defines it.


2. **A separate `SparseMiniBatchKMeans`.** Heavier, not justified, the changes are minimal in the case of adding it to the existing algorithm.
3. Using Sculley's projection algorithm. it has a hyperparameter of binary search, Duchi(2008) is cited by Sculley(2010) and return comparable results in less time in my experiments.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/9eff0fd241a2c2221112d0f7461876208e6b05d4/sklearn/linear_model/_base.py#L508

It's not expected that coefficients would have exact zeros with the supported solver 'lbfgs' for array API (although it can still happen when columns have the same value in all rows), but technically a user can still call `.sparsify()` on an estimator that was fitted to array API classes, in which case it will fail.

The documentation is not clear about limitations of LogisticRegression under array API, such as not being able to sparsify coefficients or not being able to make predictions if it somehow succeeds.

For `fit` check:

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Torch offers sparse arrays which, unlike SciPy's objects, are sub-classed from regular dense arrays:

```python
import torch
x_dense = torch.arange(10)
x_sp = x_dense.to_sparse()
isinstance(x_dense, torch.Tensor), isinstance(x_sp, torch.Tensor)
```
```
(True, True)
```

The docs for array API mention:
> PyTorch tensors can also be passed directly.
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/5b3f54b6011b736e21f4a43555e44b24bdf1d5f0/doc/modules/array_api.rst?plain=1#L118

Technically, sparse torch objects **are** torch tensors, and they appear to (unintendedly?) work under array API dispatch in some cases:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
X, y = make_classification(random_state=123)

import torch
Xt = torch.tensor(X).to_sparse()
yt = torch.tensor(y)

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression().fit(Xt, yt)
```

.. but not in every scenario where array API is supported:
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(Xt, yt)
```
```
RuntimeError: Sparse division requires a scalar or zero-dim dense tensor divisor (got shape [1] for divisor)
```

Since torch does not really implement the array API standard and does not implement `__array_namespace__` in any object class, it's not possible to make a check like "is array API" based on that, like it would be for other libraries, and technically neither the dense nor sparse tensors are array API classes, but torch is still supported.

I would expect that sparse torch tensors would not be covered under array API support, but:
* It'd nevertheless make sense to explicitly support them in some cases like `LogisticRegression` (maybe there could be a sub-section of where sparse GPU arrays could be supported).
* The error messages when passing sparse torch tensors are rather confusing. Would be ideal to get a more explicit message when sparse inputs are not supported.
* The documentation is not explicit about what happens with such inputs.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Support and lack of support for sparse torch inputs should be explicit and possible to deduce from the docs.

Whenever an array-like of string types for a multi-class classification problem is passed into the `confusion_matrix` function without an argument passed for labels, the confusion matrix is returned with the classes in alphabetical order.
While this is expected behaviour and the natural way to sort anything string-like, the outputted confusion matrix may have an output order that is different from the user's expectations, especially if the classes are ordinal. Since the output of the `confusion_matrix` function is an array, without any explicit labels, this means it will need to be manually re-aligned with the labels.

Near the start of the `confusion_matrix` function, check if the type of the arrays are string-like (or another type without an inherent order) and if `labels` is `None`, i.e. the default value. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I think there is a convergence bug in `KMeans` when empty-cluster relocation happens during an iteration.

In both `_kmeans_single_lloyd` and `_kmeans_single_elkan`, the main loop checks for strict convergence with:

```python
if np.array_equal(labels, labels_old):
    strict_convergence = True
    break
```

This check happens after the centers have been updated/swapped. If `strict_convergence` is true, the final E-step is skipped. That final E-step is otherwise used to make sure the returned `labels_` match the final `cluster_centers_`.

The problem is that empty-cluster relocation can mutate `centers_new` and `weight_in_clusters` without mutating `labels`. So `labels` can be unchanged from the previous iteration, while the centers have still changed because an empty cluster was repaired. In that case, the algorithm declares “strict convergence” even though the returned centers and labels are inconsistent.

Relevant code paths:

- `_kmeans_single_lloyd` checks `np.array_equal(labels, labels_old)` and skips the final E-step on strict convergence:
  https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py
- `_kmeans_single_elkan` has the same strict-convergence/final-E-step structure:
  https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py
- `_relocate_empty_clusters_dense` / `_relocate_empty_clusters_sparse` modify `centers_new` and `weight_in_clusters`, using `labels`, but do not update `labels`:
  https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_k_means_common.pyx

```python
for algorithm in ["lloyd", "elkan"]:

        n_clusters=3,

        n_init=1,
```

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

To ensure thread-safety, it's useful to have test infrastructure that will provide:

* A way to identify thread-safety issues in code that has previously mostly been run in process pools. Free-threading's lack of GIL makes thread safety issues more likely than in the past.
* A way to prevent _future changes_ to the code introducing new thread-safety problems.
* 🆕 A way to identify which parts of a data structure are intended to be thread-safe, and which are not.

A good starting point here is focusing on operations that are _already_ parallel, where users might reasonably expect to be able to turn threading on as a `joblib` backend and have it Just Work. These operations also work in a very particular way: create some tasks, run them in a worker pool, get back the results of the tasks.

What can go wrong in this particular idiom? Switching from a process pool to a thread pool introduces thread-safety issues with the _inputs_ to a `Parallel()` operation: whereas mutating in a process is fine, mutating in a thread can affect other threads, or future interactions with the object in the main thread.

This suggests a starting point for a invariant to be using in testing: **the inputs to a `Parallel()` operation that can correctly run with both process and thread pools should not change when the function is run.**

🆕 This invariant will not be true for objects that are _designed_ to be mutated safely, so there needs to be a way to opt out of the check.

### Describe your proposed solution

When `pytest` is run (no extra flags! 🆕) and `Parallel()`'s backend a thread pool

* Arguments passed to functions called in parallel are tracked to see if they changed as part of execution.
* "Change" is calculated heuristically, with a hash.
* If hashes change, raise an AssertionError.

🆕 There will be a mechanism to opt-out parameters, or parameter's attributes, from the hashing. In particular, they can be optionally be marked as one of:

* `thread-safe`: indicating these attributes are designed to be safely mutated from multiple threads. This should include a short explanation or pointer to explanation.
* `buggy-thread-unsafe`: indicating this is not thread-safe but is still being accessed from multiple threads. This should include a reference to a GitHub issue explaining the problem.

In addition to opt-in out of the hashing test, these will therefore also serve as documentation of thread-safety or lack thereof. They can also suggest utility classes to formalize certain idioms that repeat, e.g. one can imagine a Rust-style lock that _wraps_ an object, rather than having lock and lock-protected-object being two different parameters. Such classes would then also be automatically opted-out.

When pytest is first run with the hashing, it will fail in three ways; initial tests suggest perhaps 20 locations are affected:

* **Known thread-unsafe code:** For example, BinaryTree. This can be annotated with `ThreadSync`, with pointer to an existing issue.
* **Thread-safe code:** E.g. a result objects that is intended to used with a paired lock, an idiom used in at least one place. In this case, this can be annotated and perhaps an issue filed about formalizing the idiom into a reusable class.
* **Unknown status:** Depending how complex it is to investigate, and the investigation's conclusion, either `thread-safe` or `buggy-thread-unsafe` with issue filed to investigate it further and determine the final status.

At the end of this relatively quick process the tests should pass across the board, some new issues should be filed for follow up, and a new passing CI job can be added.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Thread sanitizers can catch some of these issues, and they should be used to validate scikit-learn thread safety over the long term. However, they are not something a developer can easily run locally: they require recompiling CPython and all relevant extensions (though there is a Docker image, but still). Whereas this approach is just a normal Python build running normal Python tests.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Process pools in sklearn will limit the number of threads used by OpenMP and BLAS. Thread pools will not set any limits.

Consider the following program, which lists how many threads are set for OpenMP/OpenBLAS/etc:

```python
import joblib, sys
from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed
import threadpoolctl

def print_thread_pool_sizes():
    for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
        print(info["user_api"], info["internal_api"], f"threads: {info['num_threads']}")

with joblib.parallel_config(backend=sys.argv[1]):
    Parallel(n_jobs=-1)([delayed(print_thread_pool_sizes)()])
```

When run under the default backend, the loky process pool, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py loky
blas openblas threads: 1
blas openblas threads: 1
openmp openmp threads: 1
```

When run under the threading joblib backend, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py threading
blas openblas threads: 20
blas openblas threads: 20
openmp openmp threads: 20
```

This can lead to significant CPU oversubscription, depending on the semantics of the library:

* When using OpenBLAS, you will get a total of 40 (20 + 20) threads, since the limit is for a single thread pool shared by the whole process.
* When using OpenMP, you will get 400 (20 * 20) threads, since the limit is _per operation starting a thread pool._

The result is code that runs slower, wasting CPU cycles, and not actually achieving any more work.

### Describe your proposed solution

There are a number of scenarios:

**Scenario 1: All cores:** If the number of threads in a thread pool is the same as the number of (available) CPU cores, setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 will work correctly: no oversubscription, no cores sitting idle.
 
**Scenario 2: All cores but 1 or 2:** If the requested number of threads/processes is negative number `-N` in joblib, this is defined as "number of available cores + 1- N". I.e. this semantically suggests the users wants to saturate the cores, but leave a few cores for other tasks. Typically N will be small, e.g. 2 to leave one core free but use all others. In this case again setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 is the right thing to do.

**Scenario 3: A hard-coded small number of cores, less than available cores:** The remaining case is most likely when the number of cores is limited due to the way the algorithm works. For process pools joblib will already automatically set the number of threads in OpenMP/BLAS to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)`. So for example if you have 10 cores and only starting a pool of size 5, OpenMP/BLAS will each be set to allow 2 threads. In a process pool, this works fine.

For a top-level thread pool, this heuristic works fine for OpenMP but _not_ OpenBLAS, since the meaning of "2" is different: for OpenMP it means "2 threads for every operation started in the 5 threads, for a total of 2 * 5 == 10 threads", for OpenBLAS it means "2 threads for the whole process, for a total of 5 + 2 threads."

So this suggests two options; one could choose one, the other, or both:

1. Documentation for algorithms with limited parallelism, suggesting that it's better to use processes in order to utilize all cores.
2. Custom settings per parallelism mechanism: set OpenMP to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)` and BLAS to `cpu_count()`. This could still lead to oversaturation in certain edge cases, but perhaps it's not as bad. 

> As a follow-up it looks like MKL at least can due OpenMP-style configuration, with a different API than the one `threadpoolctl` uses.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

This could be implemented in joblib, rather than in sklearn, but that's a more generic context; there are additional threaded libraries that it might grow support for over time, whereas sklearn has more restricted set. Still, this arguably also be done as the default joblib policy for thread pools.

### Additional context

`joblib.cpu_count()` is aware of CPU resource constraints when running inside Linux containers, so its notion of "all available cores" is usually quite accurate.

I am happy to implement this.

I have also tested this [on actual code](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_compare_reduction.html), and `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` on an all-cores thread pool makes the resulting calculation run faster and reduce involuntary context switches. This is not a perfect experiment since OpenBLAS in threaded mode is often _slower_ than single-threaded OpenBLAS for small tasks, so a better experiment would be with some code that uses OpenMP, if someone can suggest one.

There are 2 (related) things to figure out to enable callbacks to be compatible with metadata-routing. I think it's the first thing to solve before starting to implement callback support in more estimators.

- Do we want to allow passing arbitrary metadata to the callbacks ?
  ```py
  my_business_metric.set_score_request(amount=True)
  callback = ScoringMonitor(scoring=my_business_metric)
  LogisticRegression().set_callbacks(callback).fit(X, y, amount=amount)
  ```
  I'm not sure that it's very interesting for the ScoringMonitor. Do we think that anyone is interested in the evolution of a business metric during fit ?
  Same question for early stopping. Is it something that people do ?
  That being said, even if not useful for these callbacks, that may be useful for custom callbacks that I haven't thought about.

  What does that require ?
  Basically make every estimator a ``router``. And callbacks as well.
  That's not a major difficulty but it means that implementing callback support is tied to metadata-routing if you want full capacity (it might be possible to make it optional and then callbacks would be limited when there's no metadata-routing, as it's the case now)

- How to handle ``X_val`` ?
  Assuming that we do the above point, we're facing a major issue with how ``X_val`` is treated right now, that is as regular metadata. Consider the following:
  ```py
  my_business_metric.set_score_request(amount=True)
  callback = ScoringMonitor(scoring=my_business_metric, eval_on="val")
  LogisticRegression().set_callbacks(callback).fit(X, y, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val, amount_train=amount, amount_val=amount_val)
  ```
  LogisticRegression is not a consumer of ``amount``: it has no idea which one is for which set. In fact amount_train is not even useful here so I could have just passed amount=amount_val.

  X_val and y_val themselves could arguably be consumed by the estimator (at least there are estimators that transform X so X_val should follow).

  Another thing is: if we request ``amount`` on the scorer then how do we sort out how ``amount_train`` and ``amount_val`` are forwarded to the scorer ?

  All of it comes to me from the fact that ``X_val`` is considered regular metadata while it's not really metadata, it's more a secondary dataset with possibly associated metadata. I'm under the impression that the solution lies in the metadata-routing framework rather than in the callbacks, by differentiating from the start metadata associated the train set and metadata associated to the validation set.

**TL;DR** `LinearSVC(multi_class="crammer_singer")` with ≥3 classes returns a
garbage `n_iter_` and raises a spurious `ConvergenceWarning` on nearly every fit
(even at `max_iter=10_000_000`). The Crammer–Singer solver is a **single joint
optimization over all classes**, so it inherently has exactly **one** iteration
count — unlike the one-vs-rest path, which trains `nr_class` independent binary
solvers and genuinely has one `n_iter` per class. The bug is that the readout
machinery treats CS as if it were OvR with per-class counts: in
`sklearn/svm/src/liblinear/linear.cpp`, `train()` correctly allocates **one**
`int` for `model_->n_iter` in the `MCSVM_CS` branch, but `get_n_iter()` copies
`nr_class` slots — it guards the binary case (`nr_class == 2`) but not
`MCSVM_CS`, so slots `[1..K-1]` are out-of-bounds heap reads (non-deterministic
across processes). `_fit_liblinear` then warns off `max(n_iter_)`. 

One-line fix:
treat `MCSVM_CS` as a single slot in `get_n_iter()`.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

For `LinearSVC(multi_class="crammer_singer")` with three or more classes,
`clf.n_iter_` does not report the number of iterations the Crammer–Singer solver
actually ran. It reports a large, run-to-run unstable integer drawn from
out-of-bounds reads of the LIBLINEAR heap. As a downstream consequence,
`_fit_liblinear` then compares this garbage value against `max_iter` and emits
`ConvergenceWarning` on essentially every fit — including fits where the solver
converged in a few thousand epochs and `max_iter` is set to `10_000_000`.


**User-facing impact:**

- `clf.n_iter_` is not a usable signal for CS. It changes between Python
  processes (ASLR re-rolls the heap layout on each `execve`), so any code that
  inspects it — hyper-parameter search summaries, learning-curve diagnostics,
  user-written convergence checks — sees noise.
- Because the garbage almost always exceeds `max_iter`, `ConvergenceWarning`
  fires on every CS fit with K ≥ 3, even when the solver has converged. The
  recommended remedy (raising `max_iter`) doesn't help.


- Every a few times even `10_000_000` max_iter raises convergence warning.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)   # K=10 classes; any K>=3 triggers the bug

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always", ConvergenceWarning)
    clf = LinearSVC(
        multi_class="crammer_singer",
        max_iter=10_000_000,   # absurdly large — bug still fires
        random_state=0,
        dual=True,
    ).fit(X, y)
    warn_fired = any(
        issubclass(w.category, ConvergenceWarning) for w in caught
    )

print("clf.n_iter_      :", clf.n_iter_)
print("ConvergenceWarn? :", warn_fired)
```
On my machine it fires 3 out of 10 times which is obviously absurd.


**Mechanism — three cooperating defects:**

1. **Allocation site** (`sklearn/svm/src/liblinear/linear.cpp`): `train()`
   allocates exactly **one** `int` for `model_->n_iter` in the `MCSVM_CS` branch
   and writes only slot `[0]`:
   ```cpp
   model_->n_iter = Malloc(int, 1);
   // ...
   model_->n_iter[0] = Solver.Solve(model_->w);
   ```

2. **Out-of-bounds read** : `get_n_iter()` copies
   `nr_class` slots into the caller's buffer. There is a special case for
   `nr_class == 2` (the binary path, which also allocates one slot), but **no**
   case for `MCSVM_CS`:
   ```cpp
   void get_n_iter(const model *model_, int* n_iter)
   {
       int labels = model_->nr_class;
       if (labels == 2)      // binary special-cased correctly...
           labels = 1;
                             // ...but MCSVM_CS with K>=3 still loops K times
       if (model_->n_iter != NULL)
           for (int i = 0; i < labels; i++)
               n_iter[i] = model_->n_iter[i];   // slots [1..K-1] are OOB reads
   }
   ```
   
3. **Warning fired off the wrong value** (`sklearn/svm/_base.py`):
   ```python
   n_iter_max = max(n_iter_)   # dominated by heap garbage in slots [1..K-1]
   if n_iter_max >= max_iter:
       warnings.warn("Liblinear failed to converge, ...")
   ```
   `LinearSVC._classes.py` then stores `self.n_iter_ = n_iter_.max().item()`,
   exposing the same garbage value to the user as a scalar `int`.



### Expected Results


`clf.n_iter_` is a small positive integer reflecting the number of CS epochs
actually run (a few thousand on this dataset), and `ConvergenceWarning` is not
raised because the solver converged well within `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

`clf.n_iter_` is a large integer that has no relation to the number of epochs the
solver ran, and changes between Python processes. Example output on Linux x86_64
/ glibc:

```
clf.n_iter_      : 856261606
ConvergenceWarn? : True
```

The warning text is the standard one:

```
ConvergenceWarning: Liblinear failed to converge, increase the number of iterations.
```

The internal `n_iter_` buffer (the numpy array `_fit_liblinear` returns before
`LinearSVC.fit` collapses it to a scalar via `.max().item()`) shows what is
actually happening:

```
slot 0 (real epoch count) : 8401       ← solver converged; well below max_iter=10_000_000
slots 1..9 (garbage)      : [25114, 0, 0, -244463840, 232920324, 1249, 0, 2, 0]
max(n_iter_)              : 232920324  ← heap contents reinterpreted as int32; this is what becomes clf.n_iter_
```

If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This issue is a tracker for the task of adding chunking to the computation in `ledoit_wolf_shrinkage` (`sklearn/covariance/_shrunk_covariance.py`).

For the CPU implementation chunking is already supported. For the array API path we currently perform no chunking. Bigger chunks are better for GPU devices (in terms of execution time), but they require more memory.

After investigating and benchmarking a bit, I am not sure what we should do. For "tall and skinny" datasets blocking doesn't matter. For wide datasets it limits how much additional memory is used for temporaries. With `n_features=20_000` you'd use something like 1.6GB of extra memory without blocking. However, the speedup (MPS over numpy) when using blocking is much smaller than if the MPS implementation runs without blocking. It can be  5x - 10x without blocking and only something like 2x faster if you use `block_size=1000` for MPS as well.

Numpy is also faster if you increase the block size. For example, `block_size=2000` seems to speed things up by roughly a factor two and still only uses a small amount of memory.

So I think we could increase the block size, even for Numpy. But I am not sure how we should decide the trade-off between speed up and memory. We could use a block size like 3000 for all namespaces/devices to get most of the speed up and avoid catastrophic "out of memory" exceptions. The user could then tune the block size if they knew that they have enough memory? But it feels like I just made up 3000, it could equally be 4000 or 2000 - I couldn't argue which of these is more correct/better.

Quoting @ogrisel's comment here to make it easy to find:

> I suspect that for CPU devices (e.g. NumPy), the optimal block size should be set that the sum of intermediate arrays stays in Level 3 CPU cache (typically a few megabytes on most modern CPUs).
>
> It should be possible to tell if a given device is CPU or not using something like `getattr(array, "__dlpack_device__", lambda: (1, 0))()[0] in (1, 3)`.

A suggestion is to switch to using `block_size="auto"` as the default (instead of 1000). This would allow us to use a different value for different devices (eg CPUs vs GPUs). Maybe we could even determine the "best" size based on the L3 cache size, but maybe this is making things too complicated.

The `pairwise_distances` function can't always be called when using array API. We should fix this.

`pairwise_distances` with `metric="mahalanobis"` (and other scipy-delegated metrics not in `PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS`) does not work with array API inputs on non-CPU devices.

The `"mahalanobis"` metric is not in scikit-learn's `PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS`, so `pairwise_distances` falls through to the scipy fallback path, which calls `scipy.spatial.distance.cdist` / `scipy.spatial.distance.pdist`. As of scipy 1.17.1, both functions call `np.asarray()` on their inputs, which fails for GPU tensors (e.g. PyTorch MPS/CUDA, CuPy).

I'm not sure if the solution for this is to implement this in scikit-learn or wait for scipy to add support for it. For other metrics we have implementations in Python in `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py`, so maybe there is no performance downside to having a Python implementation? If yes, then this is "just" a question of turning the handle to implement new distances?

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I was debugging a problem with the skrub GapEncoder in https://github.com/skrub-data/skrub/issues/770, and I realized that the root of the problem is somewhere in the CountVectorizer, specifically when it receives a column that includes only strings of length 1 (`"A"`). 

After tracking down the problem, my understanding is that the CountVectorizer is failing because all strings in the column are shorter than the minimum value in `ngram_range` (see the example). 

The result is the exception
```
ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
```

which is not giving me a lot of information to debug. I think the error message could be improved so that it describes the situation in more detail. 

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
import string

rng = np.random.default_rng()
letters = rng.choice(list(string.ascii_letters), 1000)

# works
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
# raises ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ngram_range=(2,4)).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
```

### Expected Results

I think it makes sense that the exception is raised, so the current behavior is "expected". I would rather have a more informative error if possible, however. Something like "the vocabulary is empty because all values in the series are shorter than the minimum value of ngram_range".

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When fitting any linear model (e.g. `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `ElasticNet`) on sparse data
with `sample_weight`, the internal function `_rescale_data` is called to bake sample weights
into the data before solving. Currently it constructs an intermediate `(n_samples x n_samples)`
diagonal sparse matrix just to perform a simple row scaling, then runs a full sparse matrix
multiply through `safe_sparse_dot`.

For large sparse datasets this creates unnecessary memory allocation and computation on every
`fit()` call. The issue affects all linear models that support `sample_weight` with sparse input.

### Describe your proposed solution

Replace the `dia_array` + `safe_sparse_dot` approach with a direct elementwise row-scaling via
`csr_array.multiply()`, which is built for this exact operation and needs no intermediate matrix.

**Current code** in `sklearn/linear_model/_base.py:252`:

```python
if sp.issparse(X) or sp.issparse(y):
    sw_matrix = sparse.dia_array(
        (sample_weight_sqrt, 0), shape=(n_samples, n_samples)
    )

if sp.issparse(X):
    X = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, X)

if sp.issparse(y):
    y = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, y)
```

**Proposed code:**

```python
if sp.issparse(X):
    X = X.multiply(sample_weight_sqrt[:, None])

if sp.issparse(y):
    sw = sample_weight_sqrt[:, None] if y.ndim > 1 else sample_weight_sqrt
    y = y.multiply(sw)
```

Both produce identical results — verified against the existing `test_rescale_data` test and
directly against the old implementation across all input combinations.

**Why it is better:**

- Eliminates the `(n_samples x n_samples)` diagonal sparse matrix allocation entirely
- `csr_array.multiply(vector)` is O(nnz) with no intermediate object;
  `dia_array @ csr_array` constructs the diagonal object first, then runs a matrix-multiply
  code path
- For 100k samples: old code allocates a 100k-element `data` array and shape tuple for the
  `dia_array` before touching `X`; new code works directly on the `nnz` non-zero entries

## Describe alternatives you've considered

- `scipy.sparse.diags(sample_weight_sqrt) @ X` — same problem, still builds an intermediate
  diagonal sparse matrix
- Keeping `safe_sparse_dot` — unnecessary here since `.multiply()` handles elementwise
  scaling natively and always returns a sparse result

## Additional context

- **Affected function:** `sklearn.linear_model._base._rescale_data` (line 220)
- **Affected models:** all linear models that accept `sample_weight` with sparse `X` —
  `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `ElasticNet`, `Lasso`, and their CV variants
- **Tests:** the existing `test_rescale_data` in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py`
  already covers `sparse_container x n_targets` combinations — no new test infrastructure needed
- **Fix is ready:** branch `perf/avoid-dia-array-in-rescale-data` on fork

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The `Ridge` family is already compatible with the Array API, which is great for pytorch compatibility! It simplifies linear probing evaluations for foundation models. 

However, these models often use datasets with many examples.
It is not always feasible to accumulate features in memory before passing them to a ridge classifier.

It would be nice if `Ridge` had a `partial_fit` method which allowed processing the dataset in batches. 
With $D$ features and $N$ examples, `Ridge` would only accumulate the features statistics ($D \times D$) instead of all the features ($N \times D$)

### Describe your proposed solution

We accumulate the sufficient statistics $A = X^\top X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ and $B = X^\top Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times C}$, both of size independent of $N$. The closed-form ridge solution is $W = (A + \lambda I)^{-1} B$. Because $X$ is never materialized, memory is $O(D^2)$ instead of $O(ND)$, so the probe scales to arbitrarily large train sets.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Choose between different binning strategies ("uniform" fixed width bins, "quantile" equal mass bins) to estimate the calibration curve.

### Describe your proposed solution

Adding in `calibration_curve` a new `strategy = "uniform"` or `strategy = "quantile"` option to switch between the two binning strategies. We can for now just add the option and change the default in a follow up PR.

We can also add (in the same or follow up PR) the `strategy="isotonic"`  option to implement the CORP approach as advocated in #23132.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

There are multiple issues / PRs on implementing calibration metrics (for example the expected calibration error, the Brier score decomposition) and improving reliability diagrams:  
#18268, #11096,  #22233, #21774, #23767,  #23132

There are two main ways to estimate the calibration curve (and metrics):
1. using binning, either "uniform" (fixed-width bins) or "quantile" (equal mass bins)
2. using isotonic regression, this is the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) approach, see #23132

For the binning case, the quality of the estimate in the binning depends crucially on 
1a. the number of bins, it seems that `n_bins=n**(1/3)` is best, this is tackled by #33856
1b. the binning strategy, it seems that "quantile" is better, see [Roelofs et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08668) or [Nixon et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01685) 

Reading through the literature, I feel that the "best estimator for the calibration curve/metrics" is not yet settled.   Based on the experiments reported in the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) paper, the isotonic regression seems the most accurate. However there are ways to debias the binned estimates for the Brier score decomposition that we could investigate, see [Ferro and Fricker, 2012](https://empslocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/ferro/Publications/ferro-fricker2012copyright.pdf).

Also, we might want the different options with each its own benefits: fixed-width bins to visually compare different curves or put them in a dataframe, equal mass bins to get a more reliable curve with a manageable length (`n_bins = n**(1/3)`), isotonic regression for its accuracy but at the expense of  a crowded curve (length `n`).

Overall, having the different options seems to me the best way for further implementations of the calibration metrics or curve, without having to commit to one option over another.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When comparing classification models, users frequently need to understand how one model differs from another on a per-class basis. The current workflow requires manually computing separate confusion matrices and subtracting them:

```
cm1 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_baseline)
cm2 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_model2)
diff = cm2 - cm1
```

This pattern has no built-in support in sklearn and becomes error-prone when normalization is involved - normalizing before vs after subtraction gives different results and users may not be aware of this distinction.

There is also no standard scalable way to compare multiple models against a single baseline in one call.

### Describe your proposed solution

Add confusion_matrix_diff to sklearn.metrics with the following signature:

```
def confusion_matrix_diff(
    y_true_or_cm_baseline,
    *args,
    precomputed=False,
    labels=None,
    sample_weight=None,
    normalize=None
)
```

**Label mode (precomputed=False):**

```
# Two models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2)

# Three models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, y_pred3)

# With normalization
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, normalize='true')
```

**Precomputed mode (precomputed=True):**

`result = confusion_matrix_diff(cm_baseline, cm2, cm3, precomputed=True)`

Returns a 3D array of shape (n_comparisons, n_classes, n_classes) where:
- Positive values = comparison model better than baseline
- Negative values = baseline better than comparison model

The normalize parameter mirrors confusion_matrix exactly - normalization is applied to each matrix individually before subtraction, giving meaningful per-class rate differences rather than raw count differences.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Users can subtract confusion matrices manually, but this does not handle:
- Consistent normalization across matrices before subtraction
- Multi-model comparison in a single call
- Input validation for mismatched label sets or matrix shapes

A utility function makes this discoverable, correct by default, and consistent with the existing confusion_matrix API.

### Additional context

- No changes to existing functions — additions only
- Placement: sklearn/metrics/_classification.py alongside confusion_matrix
- Exported from sklearn.metrics
- Full numpydoc docstring and tests included in the PR

Happy to adjust the API design based on maintainer feedback before writing any code.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `StandardScaler` API reference says it Standardize features by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance and mentions `numpy.std(ddof=0)` in the "Notes" section, but does not explicitly state a mathematical equation.

For users with a statistical or mathematical background, it may be less transparent to rely on the documentation details of a third party library like NumPy than to provide a formal mathematical definition, which is easy to interpret as the difference between biased and unbiased estimators may not be immediately obvious to all users.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I propose adding the explicit LaTeX formulas for the $z$-score and the standard deviation to the "Notes" section of the `StandardScaler` docstring. This clarifies the use of the biased estimator (division by $n$) versus the unbiased estimator (also known as Bessel's correction, $n-1$), which might be a point of confusion for users.

I propose rewriting Notes as:

We use a biased estimator for the standard deviation, equivalent to ``numpy.std(x, ddof=0)``, that is:

.. math::

    s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \mu)^2}



I’d be happy to submit a PR if this approach looks good.

Hi all, this issue is to propose adding support for building scikit-learn against a SciPy install that was built with ILP64 (i.e., 64-bit integers rather than the default LP64 / 32-bit integers - see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64-bit_computing#64-bit_data_models). 

### Context

SciPy has wanted to have solid/full ILP64  support for years (efforts going back to 2020, and feature requests before that), because there are use cases and algorithms where support for large arrays where array indices don't fit in plain `int`'s is desirable. In the next SciPy release, 1.18.0, this will finally be arriving.

When building from source, there will actually be three builld modes:
1. LP64-only (default)
2. ILP64-only (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true`)
3. ILP64 for all SciPy internals, but LP64 for `linalg.blas` and `linalg.cython_blas` low-level interfaces  (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true -Dcython-blas-abi=lp64`)

See https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/building/blas_lapack.html#bit-integer-ilp64-blas-lapack for details.

Wheels on PyPI will continue to be LP64-only, so the ABI of `cython_blas` and `cython_lapack` won't be broken. However, when building from source, ILP64 can be chosen - and going ILP64-only means that downstream users of `scipy.linalg.blas|lapack|cython_blas|cython_lapack` need to work with that change.

Mode (3) can be useful as a transition mechanism for adopters (and wouldn't affect scikit-learn), but mode (2) is probably preferred. 

### Proposed solution

It is possible for scikit-learn and other downstream users to detect how SciPy was built, and adapt automatically - no new build flag will be needed in scikit-learn, it should "just work". Essentially, `scipy.linalg.cython_blas` will expose a `blas_int` that can be used. It's also not too difficult to use that conditionally when it exists, and fall back to plain `int` otherwise.

Then, there are two ways scikit-learn can go for its own Cython code:

1. Handle the change in [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx) with a small shim in each function, and keep [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd) unchanged.
2. Change `_cython_blas.pxd` as well to use `blas_int`, meaning all consumers of that interface (~15 files currently) need to be adapted as well.

It's not an either/or. Option 1 is a very localized change, and should probably be done either way. Option 2 can always be done later - it has the benefit of actually enabling use of large arrays with scikit-learn APIs as well (option 1 doesn't, because `_cython_blas.pxd` still uses `int`). So it depends on whether there's a benefit in doing that.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In `BayesianRidge`, the predictive variance calculation in the `predict` method is mathematically inconsistent with the training process when `fit_intercept=True` (the default). During `fit()`, the model centers the features (`X - X_offset_`), but during `predict()`, the variance is calculated using the **raw** test features `X_test` instead of centering them by the training mean `X_offset_`. As a result, the model reports its lowest uncertainty at the coordinate origin rather than at the center of the training data. For datasets far from the origin, this leads to significantly wrong uncertainty estimation, violating the principle that a Bayesian model should be most certain in the region where it has observed the most data. #### Mathematical formulation The original problem is $y = w^T x + b + \epsilon$. Instead, scikit-learn solves a centered version $y = w^T \tilde{x} + b' + \epsilon$, where $\tilde{x} = x - E[x]$, in order to find $w$ and $b'$, and finally $b$ is computed as $b = b' - w^T E[x]$. First, $b'$ is estimated using a frequentist approach (OLS/MLE) to be $b' = E[y]$, since $E[\tilde{x}] = 0$. This allows the problem to be reduced to $\tilde{y} = y - b' = w^T \tilde{x} + \epsilon$, on which a Bayesian approach is used to find $w$ (the posterior mean). After $w$ is found, the predictive distribution of $\tilde{y}$ on a new test point $\tilde{x}$ is then given by $$\tilde{\mu} = w^T \tilde{x}$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + \tilde{x}^T \Sigma_w \tilde{x}$$ But since $y = \tilde{y} + b'$, the predictive distribution of $y$ has the mean shifted to $$\mu = w^T \tilde{x} + b'$$ while the variance stays the same. However, our test point is actually $x$, so this all becomes $$\mu = w^T (x - \mu_x) + b' = w^T x + b$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + (x - \mu_x)^T \Sigma_w (x - \mu_x)$$ where $\mu_x = E[x]$ (estimated using the training data). Note that `predict` returns `y_mean` and `y_std`, where `y_mean` is exactly $\mu$, but `y_std` is not $\sigma$; instead it is $$\alpha^{-1} + x^T \Sigma_w x$$ What is missing is to subtract $\mu_x$ from $x$ before the variance computation. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge n = 4 x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - This issue describes a new transformer `MoveTo` that can be used to move `X` to another array namespace and device. The goal of the transformer is to move the input array `X` to a specified array namespace (numpy, torch, cupy) and device (CPU, CUDA, MPS, etc). The transformer can not move `y` or `sample_weight` but that is Ok, because of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28668.

The goal is to [enable a `Pipeline` like the following](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31274#issuecomment-2884368423) when using the experimental support for array API (and other use-cases where processing has to move from one namespace/device to another):

```python
df = pd.read_parquet("data_file.parquet")
X = df[categorical_feature_names]  # categorical or str/object dtype
y = df[target_column_name]  # continuous value to regress.

pipeline = make_pipeline(
   TargetEncoder(),  # works on categorical X but also needs y, hence CPU for both
   MoveTo(namespace=torch, device="cuda:0"),
   Ridge(),  # only numerical inputs: faster to do it all on GPU, y follows X => y_pred on GPU.
)

cv_results = cross_validate(pipeline, X, y, scoring="r2")
```

Currently you can make the example above work by replacing `MoveTo` with `FunctionTransformer(partial(torch.asarray, device="cuda:0"))`. However it is difficult for the average user to discover this particular `FunctionTransformer` incantation and looking towards the future where we want to offer a function that can "translate" a whole pipeline from running on one namespace/device to another (e.g. train on GPU, then deploy on CPU) having an explicitly named step that can be specially treated is useful.

The root cause is a violation of the "functional" requirement of the Array API specification within the _handle_zeros_in_scale helper function in sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py.

The current implementation uses in-place item assignment:

While this works for mutable backends like NumPy, it triggers a TypeError for immutable backends like JAX.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

There is quite a bit of documentation for developing scikit-learn-compatible estimators:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html

They mention for example that `__init__` should not validate parameters:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#instantiation

And they mention that calling `.fit()` should set attributes with underscores as needed:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimated-attributes

But they aren't explicit about one important detail: is the object state after fitting meant to be alterable by `.set_params()`? And if so, should that trigger re-calculations of fitted attributes for example?

For example, should the following sequences be equivalent in order for an estimator to be compatible with scikit-learn?
* `estimator.fit(...).set_output(...).predict(...)`
* `estimator.fit(...).predict(...)`

As far as I can see, most scikit-learn estimators that have some behavior that depends on input parameters after fitting make a copy of the attribute that they used with an underscore - e.g. KNN classes save an 'effective metric', PCA saves `n_components_`, and so on.

But there are cases where it doesn't work like that - e.g.:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(1000,10))

from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

LocalOutlierFactor().fit(X).set_params(novelty=True).predict(X)
# vs.
LocalOutlierFactor().fit(X).predict(X)
```

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Would be quite helpful if the doc could be more explicit about how `set_params` should or shouldn't affect the estimator state after a first call to `.fit()` has been made.

Imagine for example a case where calls to `.predict()` use different attributes according to some input parameter that's settable through `.set_params()`.

### Problem

Currently, the `n_bins` parameter in [`sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve.html) defaults to 5. This is often suboptimal for datasets of varying sizes, especially for large datasets. Users must manually tune this parameter to balance the trade-off between bias (too few bins) and variance (too many bins).

Example: for a dataset of size $n = 100,000$, the optimal number of bins is on the order of 100, far exceeding the default 5. Using the default 5 creates a calibration curve that's overly crude.

### Describe your proposed solution
Specifically, research in the paper ["Optimal Recalibration via Uniform-Mass Binning"](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3666122.3669166) provides a theoretical proof that the optimal number of bins ($B$) for recalibration via uniform-mass binning scales with the cubic root of the number of samples ($n$). (Conflict of interest: I'm an author of the paper)

The proposed implementation would be:
```python
if n_bins == 'auto':
    n_bins = int(len(y_true) ** (1/3))
```

Benefits include:
* **Ease of Use**: Tuning free. This is also the practice for many other sklearn implementation of algorithms, e.g., 
  * `max_features` of `RandomForestClassifier` defaults to `sqrt`, which uses $\sqrt{n\\_features}$ for classifiers.
  * `gamma` of `SVC` has options `'scale'` and `'auto'`.
* **Statistical Robustness**: defaulting to a theoretically optimal value improves the reliability of calibration metrics and plots across a wider range of $n$.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Maybe `'cubic-root'` or `'optimal'` will be more descriptive than `'auto'`?

### Additional context

Here's a rough description of why $\sqrt{n}$ is the optimal bin number (under some quite general assumptions):
- **Notations**: Let $Z$ be the random variable of the predicted probability to be calibrated, and $h^\star$ be the optimal calibration function $h^\star(z) := \text{E}[Y|Z=z]$. 
- **Bound of bias**: First, each bins has about $n/B$ samples, which contributes to $B/n$ factor in the calibration risk bound due to Hoeffding's inequality.
- **Bound of variance**: Then, we note the sharpness risk $\text{E}[\text{Var}(h^\star(Z)) | h(Z))]$ is the average conditional variance of $h^\star(Z)$ in each bin. Since the variance is smaller than the squared range, and the range of $h^\star(Z)$ within each bin is bounded by $O(1/B)$, we have the average conditional variance is bounded by O(1/B^2).
- **Bound of MSE**: Lastly, minimizing the sum of the two bounds $O(1/B^2 + B/n)$ yields $B \asymp n^{1/3}$.

For meta-estimators, the answer is a definitive no. They can have subestimators with callbacks which need the full context tree to work optimally.

For regular estimators, it could make sense. The performance for creating contexts is not prohibitive: ~1-2us. This is small for one iteration even for quick estimators and small datasets (knowing that callbacks don't go deeper than iterations involving the full dataset). But there might be cases where it matters.

I would avoid doing it if it adds too much verbosity within every estimator, like adding conditional branches everywhere we create a subcontext or call callback hooks. But if we can enable the feature without changing the existing callback support api implementation, why not.

### Issue Description

`sep=None` asks pandas to sniff the separator with `csv.Sniffer`, which only the python engine implements. Up to and including 2.2.3, passing `sep=None` without an explicit engine fell back to the python engine with a `ParserWarning`, and passing `engine="c"` explicitly raised a clear `ValueError`. Since 3.0.0 the fallback is gone, and the option reaches the C parser, which fails on an unhandled `None`:

```
  File "pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx", line 481, in pandas._libs.parsers.TextReader.__cinit__
    if len(delimiter) > 1:
TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()
```

Behavior on `io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n")`:

| | 2.2.3 | 3.0.0 – 3.0.5, main |
|---|---|---|
| `sep=None` (default engine) | falls back to python + `ParserWarning` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="c"` | `ValueError: the 'c' engine does not support sep=None with delim_whitespace=False` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="python"` | works | works |

The `engine="pyarrow"` case is separate but worth fixing alongside, because it fails silently rather than loudly — it ignores `sep=None` and parses each line as one column:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None, engine="pyarrow")
   a;b
0  1;2
```

The cause looks like GH-58668 (`CLN: Remove deprecated read_csv(delim_whitespace=)`, 0fc033618c7). `_clean_options` previously had:

```python
if sep is None and not delim_whitespace:
    fallback_reason = "sep=None with delim_whitespace=False"
    engine = "python"
```

When `delim_whitespace` was removed, the whole branch was deleted rather than reduced to `if sep is None:`. `_clean_options` still handles the other python-only separator cases (`len(sep) > 1`, non-encodeable `sep`), so `sep=None` is now the only one with no branch, and `engine` stays `"c"`.

This also means the documentation is currently wrong: the `sep` entry in the `read_csv`/`read_table` docstrings and in the IO user guide both still state that with `sep=None` "the Python parsing engine ... will be used", which no longer happens.

### Expected Behavior

`sep=None` with no explicit engine should fall back to the python engine and emit a `ParserWarning`, as in 2.2.3 and as the docstring describes:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None)
   a  b
0  1  2
```

`engine="c"` with `sep=None` should raise a `ValueError` naming the unsupported option, consistent with how `skipfooter` and regex separators are reported. `engine="pyarrow"` should raise rather than silently return a single column.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import io

import pandas as pd

# column "b" has one non-numeric token, so converting the first chunk raises
data = "a,b\n" + "".join(f"{i},{'oops' if i == 5 else i}\n" for i in range(20))

reader = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype={"b": "int64"}, chunksize=10)

try:
    next(reader)
except ValueError:
    pass  # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'

next(reader)  # <-- segfault
```

### Issue Description

If converting a chunk raises, the `TextFileReader` is left in a state where the
next `next()` / `get_chunk()` call segfaults instead of raising.

The exception from the first chunk is the expected one:

```
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'
```

The second call crashes the interpreter. `faulthandler` puts it inside the
Cython `TextReader.read` call:

```
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/c_parser_wrapper.py", line 234 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1923 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1985 in get_chunk
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1843 in __next__
```

Scope, from varying the reproducer (identical results on 3.0.5 and 2.3.3):

| variant | result |
| --- | --- |
| `engine="c"`, `chunksize=10` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `iterator=True` + `get_chunk(10)` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `converters=` raising on row 5 instead of `dtype=` | **segfault** |
| `engine="python"`, `chunksize=10` | raises `ValueError`, no crash |
| `engine="c"`, no `dtype=` (first chunk does not raise) | fine |

So it is specific to the C parser, and what sets it up is that a chunk raised
during conversion — `dtype=` is just a convenient way to trigger that, and a
raising `converters=` callable does it too.

Not a regression: reproduces identically on 3.0.5, on 2.3.3, and on a source
build of current `main`. Nothing string- or pyarrow-specific is involved — the
reproducer has no string column.

### Expected Behavior

The second `next(reader)` should either raise a Python-level exception or return
the remaining rows. Crashing the interpreter is never acceptable, and it is
particularly bad here because catching a per-chunk conversion error and
continuing is a natural pattern for a chunked read.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s = pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]")

s.cumsum()                                    # ArrowInvalid: overflow
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8").cumsum()  # [100, 200], dtype int64
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="Int8").cumsum()  # [100, 200], dtype Int64

# Same dtype, same data — these all upcast correctly:
s.sum()                        # 200
s.prod()                       # 10000
s.groupby([0, 0]).cumsum()     # [100, 200], dtype int64[pyarrow]
```

### Issue Description

I ran into this using int8 for the target variable in a parquet-backed training run. A cumulative bad count over a score-sorted target is how you build a gains or KS table, and with a 0/1 target the running total exceeds int8 on the 128th positive row.

`cumsum` on an integer ArrowDtype raises instead of widening the accumulator, so any series whose running total exceeds the storage width fails. Three rows of value 50 in an `int8[pyarrow]` column is enough to trigger it.
 
Every integer width is affected at its own boundary. The numpy-backed and masked equivalents widen to 64-bit and return the correct value:

| dtype | value | Arrow | numpy |
|---|---|---|---|
| int8 | 127 | ArrowInvalid | [127, 254] |
| int16 | 32767 | ArrowInvalid | [32767, 65534] |
| int32 | 2147483647 | ArrowInvalid | [2147483647, 4294967294] |
| uint8 | 255 | ArrowInvalid | [255, 510] |
| int64 | 2\*\*63-1 | ArrowInvalid | [9223372036854775807, -2] |
 
`cumprod`, `agg("cumsum")` and `Series + Series` fail the same way. `cummax` and `cummin` are unaffected, no overflow is possible.
 
But the same dtype widens correctly everywhere else. So:
 
```python
s = pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]")
s.sum()                       # 200
s.prod()                      # 10000
s.groupby([0, 0]).cumsum()    # [100, 200], int64[pyarrow]
```

So `Series.cumsum` and `SeriesGroupBy.cumsum` disagree on identical input.
 
This is present on 2.3.3 with the same pyarrow, so this is not a 3.0 regression.
 
### Root Cause:
 
`ArrowExtensionArray._accumulate` widens before accumulating, but only for temporal types
(pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py):
 
```python
convert_to_int = (
    pa.types.is_temporal(pa_dtype) and name in ["cummax", "cummin"]
) or (pa.types.is_duration(pa_dtype) and name == "cumsum")
 
if convert_to_int:
    if pa_dtype.bit_width == 32:
        data_to_accum = data_to_accum.cast(pa.int32())
    else:
        data_to_accum = data_to_accum.cast(pa.int64())
 
try:
    result = pyarrow_meth(data_to_accum, skip_nulls=skipna, **kwargs)
except pa.ArrowNotImplementedError as err:
    msg = f"operation '{name}' not supported for dtype '{self.dtype}'"
    raise TypeError(msg) from err
```
 
Integer types skip the cast and go into `cumulative_sum_checked` at their native width. The existing `except` translates `ArrowNotImplementedError` into a TypeError but does not cover `ArrowInvalid`, so the pyarrow error surfaces raw with no column or dtype context. `_reduce` already applies the upcast rule, which is why `.sum()` works on the same data.
 

### Expected Behavior

```python
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]").cumsum()
# [100, 200], dtype int64[pyarrow]
```
 
Widen narrow integer types to `int64`/`uint64` before accumulating, matching `_reduce` and the other two backends.
 
Behavior at the 64-bit boundary is a different question. numpy and masked wrap silently there (`[2**63-1, -2]`), so raising is defensible and I am not asking for it to change. The narrow widths are the part that looks unintended.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import sys

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

N = 500_000
vals = np.array([f"{'x' * 32}{i:08d}" for i in range(N)], dtype=object)
idx = pd.Index(vals, dtype="str")

reported_before = idx.memory_usage(deep=True)
idx.get_loc(idx[0])  # builds and caches the engine
reported_after = idx.memory_usage(deep=True)

held = idx._engine.values  # object-dtype copy the engine retains
unaccounted = held.nbytes + sum(sys.getsizeof(s) for s in held)

print("reported growth  :", (reported_after - reported_before) // 1000, "kB")
print("engine object arr:", held.nbytes // 1000, "kB")
print("its PyUnicodes   :", sum(sys.getsizeof(s) for s in held) // 1000, "kB")
print("unaccounted      :", unaccounted // 1000, "kB")
print("held is a copy   :", held is not np.asarray(idx._values))
```

```
reported growth  : 16908 kB
engine object arr: 4000 kB
its PyUnicodes   : 40500 kB
unaccounted      : 44500 kB
held is a copy   : True
```

### Issue Description

For an arrow-backed string Index, building the engine allocates an object-dtype
copy of the entire Index that the cached engine then holds for its lifetime, and
`memory_usage(deep=True)` accounts for none of it. Above, 16.9 MB is reported
where 61.4 MB was actually allocated — a **3.6x under-report**.

This is not just the boxed strings being missed. There are two separate gaps:

1. **`IndexEngine.sizeof()` never counts `self.values`.** For an object-dtype
   Index that is harmless, because the engine's array *is* the Index's own array
   and `_memory_usage` already counted it. But for `str`/`string[pyarrow]`,
   `_get_engine_target()` returns `vals.astype(object)`
   ([base.py#L5394](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/indexes/base.py#L5394)),
   so the engine holds a *distinct* 4 MB pointer array that nothing counts.

2. **`HashTable.sizeof()` ignores its `deep` argument entirely.** Every
   implementation in `hashtable_class_helper.pxi.in` computes
   `overhead + for_flags + for_pairs` and never looks at `deep`, so the 40.5 MB
   of `PyUnicode` objects is never counted at any setting. For object-dtype those
   strings are shared with the Index and counting them would double-count, but
   for arrow-backed string dtypes the engine owns them exclusively.

The docstring says `deep=True` includes "the memory consumption of underlying
objects referencing this Index (e.g., the characters of object-dtype values)",
and `memory_usage` deliberately adds `self._engine.sizeof(deep=deep)`, so the
intent to count the engine is clearly there — it just counts the wrong thing.

Confirmed against RSS (`psutil`), 500k keys x 40 bytes, engine build only:

| dtype | reported delta | actual RSS delta | engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| `object` | 16.9 MB | 16.9 MB | `ObjectEngine` |
| `str` | 16.9 MB | **69.4 MB** | `StringObjectEngine` |
| `string[python]` | 16.9 MB | 8.4 MB | `StringObjectEngine` |

Only the arrow-backed case is wrong: `object` matches exactly, and
`string[python]` shares `_ndarray` with the engine so nothing extra is
allocated (its RSS delta reads low only because the allocator reuses freed
pages).

It also propagates to frames — one `.loc` lookup on a string-indexed
`DataFrame` is enough:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.arange(N)}, index=idx)
df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()  # +16.9 MB reported, +69.2 MB actual
```

Since `str` is the default string dtype in pandas 3.x, this affects any
string-indexed object after its first label lookup.

### Expected Behavior

`memory_usage(deep=True)` should account for the object-dtype array the engine
retains and, for dtypes where the engine exclusively owns the boxed values, for
those values too. Concretely, `IndexEngine.sizeof` could add `self.values.nbytes`
(plus `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` when `deep=True` and the array is not shared
with the Index), or `HashTable.sizeof` could honour `deep`.

Related: GH-58529 raises the same two mechanisms — `_engine.values` not being
counted and `_engine.sizeof(deep=True)` returning nothing useful — but frames it
for `MultiIndex` and as an enhancement. Filing separately because the
arrow-backed string case is a plain under-report on a default dtype rather than
a question about which caches to include; happy for them to be merged.

```python
    assert isinstance(stack_cols, MultiIndex)
```

With `level=[0, 0]`, `set_levels` has one entry, so `stack_cols` is a plain `Index`, while
`len(level)` is still 2 and the assertion fires.

Note that the duplicates need not be written literally. `DataFrame.stack` resolves level
names and negative level numbers with `_get_level_number` before reaching `stack_v3`, so on
3-level columns `["l0", "l0"]`, `[1, -2]` and `[2, -1]` all normalize to duplicated level
numbers and hit the same code path.

This is also a change in behavior from the previous implementation, which accepted duplicate
levels and stacked sequentially:

```python
>>> df.stack([0, 0], future_stack=False)  # legacy implementation
l2       e  f
  l0 l1
0 A  c   1  2
     d   3  4
  B  c   5  6
     d   7  8

>>> df.stack(0).stack(0)  # identical result
```

### Expected Behavior

An informative exception rather than a bare `AssertionError` or an `IndexError` from an
internal `list.pop`.

There are two defensible behaviors, so I wanted to raise it rather than pick one silently:

1. **Raise an informative `ValueError`.** The current implementation stacks the specified
   original column levels simultaneously, and "the same level twice" has no meaning in that
   model. `stack_v3` already raises `ValueError("Columns with duplicate values are not
   supported in stack")` for the analogous duplicate-column case. This also avoids silently
   choosing semantics that differ from the legacy implementation, which stacked two distinct
   levels for `[0, 0]`.
2. **Deduplicate**, so that `stack([0, 0])` behaves as `stack([0])`. This would match the
   sibling APIs, which all accept duplicate levels today: `unstack([0, 0])`,
   `groupby(level=[0, 0])`, `droplevel([0, 0])` and `reorder_levels` all succeed. The
   downside is that it silently changes the legacy result rather than flagging it.

I have a PR ready implementing option 1, following the precedent of #25413, where `concat`
with `keys` was changed to raise an informative `ValueError` instead of an `AssertionError`.
Happy to switch it to option 2 if maintainers prefer consistency with `unstack`.

### Issue Description

`read_excel(engine="odf")` treats every `<table:covered-table-cell>` as empty,
without ever inspecting whether it carries its own `office:value`/
`office:value-type`. The relevant code, in
`pandas/io/excel/_odfreader.py`, `ODFReader.get_sheet_data`:

```python
if sheet_cell.qname == table_cell_name:
    value = self._get_cell_value(sheet_cell)
else:
    value = self.empty_value
```

Any cell that isn't literally a `<table:table-cell>` — i.e. any
`<table:covered-table-cell>` — takes the `else` branch and is hard-coded to
`self.empty_value`, regardless of its actual attributes.

This is usually harmless, since a covered cell is normally just a
merged-away placeholder for an ordinary row/column span with no value of its
own. But it's incorrect for the cells covered by an ODF **array/matrix
formula** (`table:number-matrix-rows-spanned` /
`table:number-matrix-columns-spanned`, [OpenDocument v1.2 Part 1, §9.1.5
`<table:covered-table-cell>`](https://docs.oasis-open.org/office/v1.2/os/OpenDocument-v1.2-os-part1.html#__RefHeading__1415592_253892949);
the attribute itself is defined in §19.680, cross-referenced e.g. in
[MS-OODF3](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/office_standards/ms-oodf3/b8bed28a-0722-4814-9e7d-2611229f5eee)):
per the OpenDocument spec, those covered cells hold their own evaluated
result, and real spreadsheet applications (verified with LibreOffice:
`soffice --headless --convert-to csv` recomputes and exports the correct
distinct value for each covered cell) read/recompute them accordingly.

I've confirmed the data is genuinely present and correctly parsed at the
odfpy layer (which pandas' odf engine is built on) — reading the same file
with `odfpy` directly via `cell.getAttrNS(office_ns, "value")` returns `"42"`
for the covered cell — so this is specific to pandas' reader wrapper, not to
odfpy or to how the file was written.


### Expected Behavior

`read_excel(engine="odf")` should read a covered cell's own `office:value`/
`office:value-type` when present, the same way `engine="calamine"` already
does, instead of unconditionally treating it as empty. At minimum, a covered
cell that carries an explicit `office:value` should not silently lose it.
